content: Checkpoint-based localisation is a first-class positioning method, not a degraded version of continuous tracking, and the literature says so explicitly. Sartayeva et al., 'A Survey on Indoor Positioning Security and Privacy' (PolyU), describes QR-code landmarking as 'the simplest instance of proximity-based positioning' which 'provides snapshots of people's locations, meaning that QR code landmarking on its own is not capable of tracking people in real-time'. The standard indoor-positioning vocabulary for a stale fix is 'last known position' (LKP): indoor systems that fuse beacons with dead reckoning treat the LKP as the anchor that inertial/pedestrian dead reckoning is corrected against, and the academic literature quantifies the resulting error (PDR step-length error 2.8-7 percent over 150m, i.e. 5-8m of drift). The honest framing for this project is therefore 'checkpoint navigation with a last-known-position model': position is exact at scan instants and unknown between them, error grows with distance from the last scan, and the only honest way to describe it is a bounded-error statement, not a 'live location'. Notably, no indoor positioning survey claims QR landmarking gives continuous tracking, so an examiner comparing the project against the literature will find the over-claim unsupported. Google Maps' own Navigation SDK FAQ models the equivalent problem outdoors: it shows 'Searching for GPS...' after 10 seconds without a fix and keeps the chevron at the last known signal rather than pretending to know where it is - the industry-standard precedent is to show a stale marker plus an explicit signal-loss state, not to interpolate silently.
